title: Egypt and the Nile
hook: Amr ibn al-As enters Egypt in 640, and over centuries Egypt becomes mostly Muslim

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people of the ship, and the Prophet's word that they had made two hijrahs. Your line was: africa sheltered them first. Did you thank someone who once sheltered you? Day nine hundred sixty-six.

Remember the envoys from Mecca who sailed to Abyssinia with gifts for the Negus, hoping he'd hand the refugees back? Ibn Ishaq names one of them: Amr ibn al-As. He went home empty-handed. Later he became a Muslim himself, and a commander. And one day, under the caliph Umar, he leads an army west out of Palestine, across the edge of the desert, toward a green river valley that had been home to kings, temples and churches long before. Today's words: Egypt and the Nile.
screen: `AN ENVOY TO THE NEGUS.` → `NOW A MUSLIM COMMANDER.` → `WEST, TOWARD THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Egypt in Arabic is Misr, the same name the Qur'an uses in the story of Yusuf, where Egypt is the land that takes him in and where, in the end, his whole family comes to live. When Amr's army arrived, Egypt was ruled from Constantinople, and in its towns and villages the Arab soldiers met Coptic Christians. Amr took the fortress beside the Nile, and later Alexandria by the sea. Then he founded a new town on the river bank, called Fustat, and built a mosque there. It has been rebuilt again and again, and it still carries his name: the mosque of Amr ibn al-As. Before any of this, a hadith in Sahih Muslim says, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions that they would one day enter Egypt, and asked them to treat its people well, because they had a claim of protection and of kinship. Scholars explain the kinship through Hajar, the mother of Ismail, and through Mariyah the Copt, the mother of the Prophet's son Ibrahim. And here is the part that's easy to get wrong. Egypt did not become Muslim when Amr arrived. Historians describe a slow change. Over generations, more and more Egyptians became Muslim, through marriage, through trade, through the pull of the cities, through taxes and law, through faith. Arabic slowly became the language of the street. And Coptic Christians stayed. They are still there, in their churches, and the old Coptic language is still sung in their liturgy. Hence the line: slowly, over centuries. A country's faith didn't change in a battle. It changed in kitchens and markets, one family at a time, across lifetimes.
screen: `MISR — THE LAND THAT TOOK YUSUF IN.` · `AMR, FUSTAT, AND A MOSQUE.` · `TREAT ITS PEOPLE WELL: PROTECTION AND KINSHIP.` · `COPTS STAYED, AND STILL SING.` · then, large: `SLOWLY, OVER CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one Egyptian mosque. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the mosque of Amr ibn al-As in old Cairo: a broad open courtyard under the sky, rows of columns holding up the roof, the noise of the city outside its walls. Rebuilt again and again, and still in use, near the river where it began. Hold that picture: one building, prayed in by generations who each added a little. If you pray, you can make a dua for the people who pray there now. If you don't, simply hold the place in mind. The bell holds the time.
Egypt and the Nile. Misr, the land of Yusuf, which Amr ibn al-As entered, and where, slowly, families became Muslim beside Coptic neighbors. Today's words.
Your line: slowly, over centuries. Today, find one photo of the mosque of Amr ibn al-As, and notice one detail you didn't expect. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims in Egypt pray in mosques old and new, including the mosque of Amr ibn al-As in Cairo, and live alongside Coptic Christian neighbors whose churches go back to before Islam.

trapdoor: what you thought: an army arrived and Egypt became Muslim.
what it means: Amr ibn al-As entered Egypt, and over centuries, family by family, more Egyptians became Muslim, while Copts remained.
what a scholar hears: Fustat and the mosque of Amr, the hadith of protection and kinship in Sahih Muslim, and Coptic still sung in the liturgy.

sources.ref: Qur'an 12:21, 12:99 (Misr in the story of Yusuf)

notes: No date given for Amr's entry into Egypt (the index hook says 640) and no population figures, under the claims rule; the index's 'mostly Muslim' is rendered as 'more and more Egyptians became Muslim'.
Amr ibn al-As as one of the envoys to the Negus is from Ibn Ishaq; day 743 left the envoys unnamed. Confirm.
Sahih Muslim 2543 paraphrased ('dhimmah and rahim'); the explanation through Hajar and Mariyah is attributed to scholars. Confirm numbering and wording.
Misr in the Qur'an: 12:21 and 12:99 cited; confirm.
Reasons for gradual conversion (marriage, trade, cities, taxes and law, faith) are listed without ranking; confirm the list is fair and not overstated.
The mosque of Amr described generally (courtyard, columns, rebuilt many times, still in use); confirm.
Editor: the practice's 'look up a picture' duplicated the carry, so it was cut from the practice; varied the stock 'That's today's line'.

Audit (y3 957-966): Mariyah's status (wife or umm walad) is debated among Muslim scholars; 'the Prophet's Coptic wife' changed to 'Mariyah the Copt, the mother of the Prophet's son Ibrahim' in the teach and the match pair. Keeper to confirm.
